submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires on a noun phrase that 'of' binds to a complement it belongs to: the noun-internal 'of' itself, the head noun just before it, and the determiner that follows it ('the head of the department' 0.6/1.2/1.0, 'those of earlier studies' 1.5), and it stays at the floor where 'of' instead completes a verb or a fixed idiom ('accused them of theft', 'consists of water', 'died of cancer', 'approved of the plan'). The same 'of' is much weaker when the phrase is introduced by a possessive or indefinite determiner rather than 'the' ('our head of ...' about zero, 'a head of ...' about half of 'the head of ...'), and its strength is graded by how tightly the head noun names a part or attribute of the complement ('head/top/back/beginning of' 0.6-1.2 versus 'author/colour/name of' 0.1-0.4).

adversarial_test_results.prompt: They accused the manager of theft after the quarterly audit.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Verb-selected 'of' with a bare noun complement ('accused ... of theft'); the hypothesis says 'of' that completes a verb stays at the floor, so it predicts no activation.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: After a long debate, the board approved of the plan.
adversarial_test_results.detail: This is the hypothesis's own floor pattern ('approved of the plan'): 'of the' follows a verb rather than a head noun, so the hypothesis predicts inactivity.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: He spoke of the war years with obvious affection.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Verb-selected 'of the' after 'spoke' reproduces the exact 'of the' surface of the activating examples, but 'of' completes the verb, which the hypothesis says stays at the floor.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Her grandfather died of pneumonia last winter.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The hypothesis explicitly lists 'died of cancer' as a floor case; 'died of pneumonia' has the same verb-bound 'of', so it predicts no activation.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: In spite of the rain, the match continued until dusk.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The compound preposition 'in spite of the' supplies the same 'of the' surface as the activating examples but is a fixed idiom, which the hypothesis predicts stays at the floor.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: For years the children had been afraid of the dark cellar.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Adjective-selected 'afraid of the' gives 'of the' plus a definite noun but no part/attribute head noun, so the hypothesis predicts the floor.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: When she opened it, the box was full of old photographs and letters.
adversarial_test_results.detail: 'full of' is an adjective complement rather than a noun-internal binding, so the hypothesis predicts inactivity despite the 'of'.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Our head of department resigned without warning.
adversarial_test_results.detail: The hypothesis says a possessive determiner introducing the phrase ('our head of ...') is about zero, so this near-copy of 'the head of the department' is predicted inactive.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Yesterday the department head and several members met to discuss the merger.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Contains the claimed activating words 'head' and 'members' but no 'of' binding at all, so the hypothesis predicts the token-level confound is silent.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Hippocampal responses differed from those in the perirhinal cortex during the recognition test.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Same neuroscience topic and the same 'those' head as top examples 2, 4 and 6, but with 'in' instead of 'of'; the hypothesis is about 'of' binding, so it predicts inactivity.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Most of the students passed the exam easily.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Quantifier partitive 'most of the' has the 'of the' surface but 'most' is a fused quantifier rather than a part/attribute noun, so the hypothesis predicts the floor.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: Even in winter the city of Rome attracts millions of visitors.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Noun-internal 'of' in an appositive ('the city of Rome') where the complement names the entity rather than a whole the head belongs to, so the hypothesis's part/attribute condition is not met and it predicts the floor.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
At seven in the morning the site office opened and the safety team began its quarterly inspection. The lead inspector, a former rigger named Marsh, walked the perimeter first, checking the fencing, the scaffold tags and the fire points. Behind him an apprentice recorded each observation on a tablet and photographed everything that would need attention before the crew arrived. The morning was cold and the ground still held water from the weekend, so the two men moved slowly and avoided the muddy stretches near the excavation. A lorry reversed into the loading bay, its alarm beeping across the yard, and the apprentice noted that the reversing lights were filthy and half hidden behind stacked pallets.

Many workers had been on this site since spring, and several had raised concerns about the temporary walkway beside the loading bay. Marsh measured the gap between the handrail and the wall, noted that it fell short by a few centimeters, and asked the site manager to close the route until a proper barrier could be installed. The manager agreed, though he complained of the cost and the delay. He said the walkway had been fine for months and that nobody had been hurt. Marsh replied that a standard does not depend on whether anyone has been hurt yet. Beyond the fence parked cars glittered under the early sun, and a dog barked at a cyclist on the path beside the canal.

The inspection then moved to the east tower, where the concrete pour was scheduled for the following day. Marsh climbed the stairs to the third floor and watched a crew tying reinforcement bars. He asked one worker to show him the certificate for the crane, and the man could not produce it. The operator was called over and explained that the paperwork was in the main office and would be sent by email before noon. Meanwhile the apprentice measured the stairwell with a tape and found the width acceptable, though the lighting was poor and the handrail had worked loose at one bracket. The tower was wrapped in green netting, and the wind rattled a loose panel.

Later, over a hurried lunch, the inspectors reviewed their notes and agreed that the permit for the tower crane should be suspended until the certificate arrived. The site manager argued, then relented, and the crew was sent home early. In his report Marsh wrote that the contractor had failed to keep the required documentation and that the crane had been operated without valid certification. He recommended a full audit, and near the end he accused the company of negligence in its record keeping. The company had won the contract on a low bid, and the schedule had been tight from the start. The regional office would decide by Friday whether to approve of the recommendation, and the file would sit on a desk for another three weeks before anyone read it.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A long passage (well over 512 tokens) whose ' of' tokens are all verb-selected ('complained of the cost', 'accused the company of negligence', 'approve of the recommendation'), placed deep in the text; the hypothesis predicts the floor throughout.

adversarial_test_results.detail: Recipe/procedural genre holdout: 'the base of the tin' is a tight part noun with a definite determiner, so the hypothesis predicts activation.

adversarial_test_results.detail: The head noun is still introduced by 'the' while the complement is introduced by possessive 'our'; the hypothesis's weakening clause is about the head's determiner, so it predicts this still fires.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
When the reading room closed at six, Elara wheeled the boxed manuscript to the conservation bench and switched on the lamp. The parchment had spent decades in a damp cellar, and the damage was worse than the catalogue entry suggested. She began by recording the condition of each gathering in a notebook, noting every tear, stain and wormhole in a fine pencil. The leather binding had cracked along the spine, and several quires had worked loose from the sewing. Before any treatment could begin, the curator wanted a complete photographic record, so Elara raised the camera above the bench and adjusted the lights until the raking angle revealed the texture of the surface without washing out the faded ink.

The first folio was the hardest. Its lower margin had been trimmed by a later owner, and a column of text had vanished where the leaf was repaired with paper that did not match. Elara laid the leaf on a sheet of silicone and humidified it slowly, working inward from the outer edge. She had learned, after many small disasters, that haste was the enemy of parchment. Once the fibers had relaxed, she turned the leaf over and examined the reverse, where a faint sketch of a dragon ran along the gutter. She compared the repaired area with a reference photograph, checking the alignment of the fibers and the tone of the ink.

By mid-evening the studio had grown quiet enough that she could hear the old building settle. She lifted the leaf with a spatula and laid it flat on the felt, then began the tedious work of mending the tears with wheat starch paste and strips of Japanese tissue. Her tweezers moved along the corner of the page, lifting a fragment no larger than a grain of rice and setting it into place. The work demanded a kind of attention that shut out everything else, and she did not notice the hour until the clock in the corridor struck eleven. Outside, the street lamps came on one by one, and a bus sighed past on the wet road.

The conservator would need photographs, measurements and a note for every intervention, but that work could not be finished tonight. The exhibition had been planned for two years, and the curator had promised the manuscript to the publicity office before anyone had examined it. Elara did not envy him that conversation. The condition of the binding alone would require a case with a custom cradle, and the mounts would need to be built by a specialist in the spring. She had already warned him that the ink on several leaves was flaking, and that any movement could cost the library a line of text that no photograph could recover.

Elara covered the manuscript with a weighted board, turned off the lamp, and walked out past the glass cases where the library's rarest volumes slept under low light. At the far end of the gallery she paused with her hand on the handle of the door and looked back once at the darkened room. In the morning the curator would ask whether the treatment could be finished before the exhibition opened, and Elara would have to explain, again, that parchment keeps its own schedule and that the corners of a fragile page cannot be hurried.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Long literary passage (over 512 tokens) with several 'the X of the Y' part/attribute bindings, including 'the corner of the page' and 'the handle of the door' deep in the text; the hypothesis predicts activation.
